output.query: alcohol-related brain damage versus behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia

results.finding: Alcohol-related brain damage causes executive and memory impairment with frontal and cerebellar volume loss; deficits stabilise or partly recover with sustained abstinence.
results.source: Ridley NJ, Draper B, Withall A. Alcohol-related dementia: an update of the evidence. Alzheimers Res Ther 2013;5:3

results.finding: Proposed criteria for alcohol-related dementia require heavy use for at least five years and a cognitive diagnosis made at least 60 days after the last drink.
results.source: Oslin D, Atkinson RM, Smith DM, Hendrie H. Alcohol related dementia: proposed clinical criteria. Int J Geriatr Psychiatry 1998;13:203-212

results.finding: In people who drink heavily, Wernicke encephalopathy is diagnosed clinically by two of four Caine criteria and is treated with parenteral thiamine.
results.source: Galvin R et al. EFNS guidelines for diagnosis, therapy and prevention of Wernicke encephalopathy. Eur J Neurol 2010;17:1408-1418

output.summary: Alcohol-related brain damage produces executive and memory deficits with frontal and cerebellar volume loss that stabilise or partly recover with abstinence, whereas a neurodegenerative syndrome continues to progress; proposed criteria therefore defer the cognitive diagnosis until at least 60 days after the last drink. Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis in heavy drinkers (two of four Caine criteria) treated with parenteral thiamine.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls (a supervised alcohol-withdrawal regimen is a separate indication).
Do not prescribe disulfiram: with impaired impulse control and judgement a disulfiram-alcohol reaction is likely.
Do not attribute the entire syndrome to alcohol: the frontotemporal lobar pattern and behavioural phenotype indicate a primary neurodegenerative process.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state the features present (disinhibition, loss of empathy, perseverative behaviour, executive-predominant neuropsychological profile), the functional decline (dismissal, financial judgement), and the level of certainty (probable, given the disproportionate frontal atrophy).

Explain why alcohol-related brain damage and untreated sleep apnoea do not account for the whole progressive syndrome, treat both, and reassess cognition and behaviour after sustained abstinence and CPAP use to separate a reversible component from progressive bvFTD.

Give parenteral high-dose thiamine, before any glucose-containing fluid, because cerebellar signs with cognitive impairment in a heavy drinker meet two Caine criteria for Wernicke encephalopathy (EFNS 2010), then continue oral thiamine; refer to addiction services for supported abstinence.
Address safety and capacity: driving (alcohol and impaired judgement), finances (the $30,000 investment; protect accounts and discuss lasting power of attorney while he has capacity).
Arrange caregiver education and support for his wife, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.
Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, given onset at 60 and his mother's dementia from her late 50s, and discuss what a result would mean for his son.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not part of the FTD work-up; FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT is the functional study when one is needed.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, sporadic, with concurrent alcohol use disorder and alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration (comorbid contributor)

differential.diagnosis: Alcohol-related brain damage as the sole cause
differential.key_features: For: heavy drinking, macrocytosis, raised GGT and transaminases, cerebellar atrophy. Against: loss of empathy and perseveration, primitive reflexes, and lobar frontal atrophy disproportionate to the rest of the brain. Course after sustained abstinence decides.

Ataxia with cognitive impairment meets two Caine criteria, so thiamine is given; against it as the cause: two-year progressive behavioural course, no ophthalmoplegia or confusion, preserved recognition memory, normal mammillary bodies.
Grandiosity and an uncle's psychiatric admission raise it; against it: no episodic mood elevation, progressive decline with loss of empathy, executive profile and frontal atrophy.
Reduced delayed recall at the bedside; against it: preserved recognition memory and hippocampi, posterior cortical sparing. An amyloid or CSF AD biomarker is optional if doubt remains.
Hypertension and Fazekas 2 white matter change; no infarcts, and the lobar frontal atrophy and behavioural phenotype are not explained by small-vessel disease.

key_clinical_evidence: Three Rascovsky features on the wife's history (disinhibition, loss of empathy, perseverative behaviour), an executive-predominant neuropsychological profile with preserved recognition memory, and dismissal after a 28-year unblemished career.
MRI: moderate bilateral frontal atrophy disproportionate to temporal and posterior cortex, with normal mammillary bodies.

Macrocytosis, raised GGT and transaminases and cerebellar vermian atrophy mark a comorbid alcohol-related contribution; reassessment after sustained abstinence separates a reversible deficit from progression.
Cerebellar signs with cognitive impairment in a heavy drinker call for empiric parenteral thiamine.
His mother's dementia from her late 50s supports offering genetic counselling; testing is optional.

behavioural variant frontotemporal demen.query: behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia diagnostic criteria and management

results.finding: Three of six core features within the first three years define possible bvFTD. Probable bvFTD requires functional decline and supportive imaging.
results.source: Rascovsky K et al. Brain 2011;134:2456-2477 (FTDC criteria for bvFTD)

results.finding: Primary psychiatric disorders are the commonest misdiagnosis. No disease-modifying treatment is available.
results.source: Bang J, Spina S, Miller BL. Frontotemporal dementia. Lancet 2015;386:1672-1682

behavioural variant frontotemporal demen.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. Psychiatric disorders are the main mimics and are excluded on course and examination rather than on a single test. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD with concurrent alcohol use disorder and alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration. Teaching: escalating drinking can accompany the behavioural change of bvFTD; loss of empathy, perseveration and disproportionate frontal atrophy point beyond alcohol, and the course after sustained abstinence separates the reversible component. Cerebellar signs with cognitive impairment call for parenteral thiamine. Disulfiram is unsafe when impulse control is impaired.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W is a 62-year-old former financial advisor who presents with his wife after being referred by his internist for cognitive evaluation. His wife describes a 2-year history of progressive personality changes that have been difficult to separate from his escalating alcohol use. He was terminated from his financial advisory position 18 months ago following several compliance violations — he had been making unauthorized trades in client accounts and dismissing colleagues' concerns about policy violations with dismissive and sometimes belligerent responses. He has never acknowledged that these violations were his fault, insisting he was 'unfairly targeted.' Prior to this, he had a 28-year career without any disciplinary record. At home, he has become increasingly impulsive — making a $30,000 investment in a scheme his wife considers fraudulent, and responding with rage when questioned. He now drinks 4-6 drinks daily by his report; his wife estimates 8-10. He has become grandiose, making claims about his business acumen that are not consistent with his recent performance. He has lost empathy — when his son had a significant health scare, he expressed no concern. He has become highly perseverative in arguments — repeating the same accusations against his former employer in every conversation for 18 months. His sleep apnea is moderate-severe and he abandoned his CPAP after two weeks. He has a family history of possible dementia in his mother (onset her late 50s) and possible psychiatric institutionalization in his maternal uncle. His behavioral changes have unfolded over the same period as the escalation in his drinking.
